title: Sign for this one?
topic: Probity in records, forms and certification
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a surgical ward. In your trust, doctors can act as the second witness for controlled drugs. Leah, a staff nurse, asks you to countersign the controlled drug register for a dose of oral morphine she gave two hours ago.

You weren't there when it was given. She says, "It was really busy and no one was free to check it."
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Sign it, as you trust her and the stock count is correct.
options.detailed: A correct count doesn't mean you witnessed the dose. Your signature would be untrue.

options.text: Explain that you can't sign for a dose you didn't see.
options.brief: Signing would make the register inaccurate.
options.detailed: Your signature confirms you witnessed the dose being checked and given. Signing now would create a false record.

options.text: Suggest she tells the nurse in charge.
options.brief: The person running the shift needs to know.
options.detailed: The nurse in charge can decide what to do, including how to record it accurately and whether staffing needs escalating.

options.text: Sign it with today's time, so the record looks complete.
options.detailed: This deliberately misrepresents what happened, which is dishonest.

options.text: Report her to the Nursing and Midwifery Council.
options.detailed: A single missed check on a busy shift should be handled locally, not by the regulator.

options.text: Ask another doctor to sign it instead.
options.brief: Moves the false record to someone else.
options.detailed: No one witnessed the dose, so anyone who signs creates a false record.

options.text: Ask pharmacy to recount every controlled drug on the ward.
options.detailed: There is no suggestion of a discrepancy. A ward-wide recount doesn't address the missed check or the request to sign.

options.text: Suggest the missed check is reported as an incident.
options.brief: Lets the trust learn from it.
options.detailed: A controlled drug given without the required check is a reportable incident. Reporting it supports learning about the staffing pressures behind it.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you keep records honest when a colleague asks you to sign for something you didn't witness.
explanation.keyDetails: You didn't see the dose given. The ward was busy. She is asking you to countersign after the event.
explanation.reasoning: [B] keeps the record honest, [C] involves the nurse in charge, and [H] supports learning. The distractors falsify the record ([A], [D], [F]), or overreact ([E], [G]).
explanation.competing: [F] might seem to solve the problem, but no one witnessed the dose, so any signature would be false.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 4, making sure the records you sign are accurate.
